Selfwilled
self'wild
adj. (self-pleasing, governed by one's own will; expressly disqualifying in an elder)
The Authorized Version's compound for Greek authades — from autos (self) and hedomai (to please) — one who pleases himself, arrogant, unaccommodating. The English keeps the sense exactly: a will that answers to itself.

Biblical Definition

“For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre” (Titus 1:7). The disqualification is placed immediately after the word steward, and that is the argument. A steward manages what belongs to another; a selfwilled man manages what belongs to another as though it belonged to him. Paul then gives the positive side: “But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate” (Titus 1:8), and requires him to hold fast the faithful word so that he can exhort and convince the gainsayers (Titus 1:9). The only other occurrence of the word is a description of false teachers: “Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities” (2 Peter 2:10). Peter sharpens it by contrast in the next verse — angels, who are greater in power and might, “bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord” (2 Peter 2:11). The selfwilled man is bolder than an angel and has less warrant.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines self-willed as governed by one's own will, not yielding to the will or wishes of others, obstinate.

expand to see more

SELF-WILLED, a. Governed by one's own will; not yielding to the will of others; obstinate.

SELF-WILL, n. One's own will; obstinacy.

STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and receive and pay money.

PRESUMPTUOUS, a. Bold and confident to excess; adventuring without reasonable ground of success.

OBSTINATE, a. Stubborn; fixed firmly in resolution or opinion; not yielding to reason or persuasion.

Key Scripture

Titus 1:7 — "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;"

2 Peter 2:10 — "But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities."

Titus 1:8 — "But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate;"

2 Peter 2:11 — "Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord."

Modern Corruption

Self-will is rebranded as strong leadership, and the very trait Scripture bars from the office becomes the reason a man is given it.

expand to see more

The contemporary vocabulary of church leadership — vision, decisiveness, the willingness to make hard calls without consensus — describes something Scripture may commend and something Scripture expressly forbids, and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the outside. Titus 1:7 supplies the test, and it is the word steward. A steward has authority and the authority is delegated; he answers for the estate to someone else. A man who cannot be told anything, who treats the plurality of elders as an obstacle, and whose congregation has learned that disagreement is disloyalty, is not a strong leader with rough edges. He is disqualified by the text, whatever the church has grown to.

The plurality of elders is the structural safeguard the New Testament provides against exactly this, and it is the safeguard most often quietly dismantled — retained on paper while one man's will decides everything of consequence. Peter's picture is the check on the other end: angels greater in power do not bring railing accusation, and the selfwilled teacher does. Boldness is not evidence of authority. The measure of a steward is whether he can be corrected by the Word and by the brethren the Lord has set beside him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek authades (G829), self-pleasing — Titus 1:7, 2 Peter 2:10; contrasted with oikonomos (G3623), a steward — Titus 1:7.

expand to see more

Greek authades (G829) — self-pleasing, arrogant; only Titus 1:7 and 2 Peter 2:10, and disqualifying in both.

Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a house-manager, steward; Titus 1:7, 1 Corinthians 4:1-2, where the requirement is faithfulness.

Greek tolmetes (G5113) — a daring man, presumptuous; 2 Peter 2:10, joined to authades.

Greek plektes (G4131) — a striker; Titus 1:7 and 1 Timothy 3:3, the physical companion of a self-pleasing temper.

Titus 1:8 gives the positive portrait the negative list is measured against — hospitable, sober, just, holy, temperate.

Usage

"“A bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled” — the steward is the test."

"“Presumptuous are they, selfwilled” — the mark of the false teacher."

"Angels greater in power bring no railing accusation; the selfwilled man does."
